solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Credit parties on the right for this country heading left

indicators.note: in an across answer, going left means reading right to left

blocks.note: the setter's country, the United Kingdom
a do is a party, so dos are parties

explanation.surface: A political report: parties on the right are taking credit while the country drifts left.
explanation.walkthrough: The political words 'parties', 'right' and 'left' are all positional here, telling you where the pieces go and which way UK reads.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the credit you get for an achievement is the kudos it brings.

clue.text: Garment somewhat like trousers to the north?

indicators.note: to trouser something is to pocket it, so these words keep the answer tucked inside
in a down answer, heading north means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: the letters T LIK run across the join of somewhaT LIKe

explanation.surface: Someone describes a Scottish garment as a bit like trousers, the kind worn up north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' looks like part of the description of the garment, but it is a verb here meaning pockets. The surface also gets a joke out of the kilt being worn in the north of Britain, in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A kilt is a pleated knee-length skirt, the traditional Scottish garment.

clue.text: Circus flier paid for with words overlapping was shocking

definitions.note: the definition is a verb phrase; DUMBFOUNDED means shocked, but 'was shocking' can be read as 'was dumbfounding'

indicators.note: the two words overlap, so the last letter of the first ends up sitting inside the second

blocks.note: Dumbo is Disney's flying circus elephant
to fund something is to pay for it

explanation.surface: A circus trapeze act, paid for with an argument going on over it, turns out to be shocking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' suggests a trapeze artist, but the circus flier is Disney's elephant. The two words overlap rather than simply join, the tail of the first sliding into the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Dumbfounded means so astonished as to be speechless.

clue.text: Quiet monastery rejects European in poor order

blocks.note: sh is the call for quiet
an abbey is a monastery
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A silent monastery turns away a European visitor, all in poor order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In poor order' looks like a comment on how the rejection was carried out, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something shabby is worn out and in poor condition.

clue.text: Beautiful doctor that I see with heart of ice

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are altered
the heart of ICE is its middle letter

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters
C is the middle letter of ICE

explanation.surface: Someone describes a handsome doctor they have been seeing, who has a cold heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' reads as a noun, the attractive man in question, but it is the verb that shuffles the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesthetic can mean pleasing to look at, beautiful.

clue.text: A lustful look secures kiss with conquering king

indicators.note: the look secures the kiss by holding it inside

blocks.note: A is used as it stands
a leer is a lustful look
X is the kiss at the end of a letter
and means together with

explanation.surface: A lecherous glance that wins a kiss from a king used to conquest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' looks like a link word joining the look to the king, but it supplies letters, and it goes inside the look alongside the kiss.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander the Great was the Macedonian king who conquered much of the known world.

clue.text: Reversible pieces?

blocks.note: not clothing you can turn inside out, but a word that reads the same backwards
musical pieces, each for a single performer

explanation.walkthrough: 'Reversible' suggests clothes you can wear inside out, but it means the word itself reads the same backwards. The pieces are musical ones, performed alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Solos are musical pieces for one performer, and SOLOS is a palindrome.

clue.text: Place full of detectives after one?

definitions.text: Place full of detectives after one?

indicators.note: the place is full of the detectives, so they sit inside it
the detectives come after the one, so I goes first

blocks.note: a home is a place, as in 'come round to my place'
I is the Roman numeral one
the CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, Britain's plain-clothes detectives

explanation.surface: A police station swarming with detectives, all chasing one suspect.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue is a police department with detectives chasing a killing: 'one' is both the letter I and a single murder they are after.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes the homicide squad, a police unit of detectives who go after killings, the crime also called homicide.

clue.text: Horn’s sound not fully included

indicators.note: the sound is not given in full, so it loses its last letter

blocks.note: a toot is the sound a horn makes

explanation.surface: A horn's note that gets only partly into a recording.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Included' is the definition in the sense of 'as well': if you are included, you are coming too.
explanation.definitionFit: Too means also, as in 'me too', meaning I am included.

clue.text: Very fine sugar excited fly during prison picnic

indicators.note: an excited fly buzzes about, so its letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the can is slang for prison
anagram fodder, 3 letters
a picnic, like a doss, is something easy to do

explanation.surface: A fly gets excited about the sugar at an outdoor meal in a prison yard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picnic' is not food here but its slang sense of a doddle; a doss is a British word for an easy task.
explanation.definitionFit: Candyfloss is spun sugar, so fine it forms a fluffy cloud; Americans call it cotton candy.

clue.text: As you’ll hear, fabrication produced sharp pop

indicators.note: the answer is what you hear when the phrase is spoken

blocks.note: a fabrication is a lie, and produced is made

explanation.surface: A report that a made-up story produced a sudden sharp bang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sharp pop' sounds like a noise, but pop is a fizzy drink and sharp describes its sour taste.
explanation.definitionFit: Limeade is a lime-flavoured soft drink, tart and fizzy.

clue.text: Send up balloon with light for the party

indicators.note: the light goes in for, meaning in place of, the party

blocks.note: used as it stands, before the swap
a lamp is a light
a ball is a party, and it is the start of BALLOON

explanation.surface: Instructions to release a balloon with a light on it for a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Send up' looks like launching the balloon, but it means to mock.
explanation.definitionFit: To lampoon is to send up, to ridicule someone in satire.

clue.text: A boy fancies it, playing for club on the left wing

indicators.note: letters that are playing are moving about, not in their places

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

explanation.surface: A boy dreams of turning out for a football club as its left winger.
explanation.walkthrough: The football words, 'playing', 'club' and 'left wing', all turn political: the club is a society, and the left wing is the political left.
explanation.definitionFit: The Fabian Society is a British socialist society, a club of the political left linked to the Labour Party.

clue.text: Situation of five triathlons in ten after cycling

indicators.note: the five triathlons go inside the ten
TEN is cycled, its first letter moved to the end to give ENT

blocks.note: V is the Roman numeral five
Ironman races are long triathlons
used as it stands, then cycled to ENT

explanation.surface: Five triathlons crammed into ten days after a cycling stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' is naturally a leg of a triathlon, but it tells you to move the T of TEN to the back.
explanation.definitionFit: Your environment is your surroundings, the situation you are in.

clue.text: Peanuts perhaps son dropped in journey through the universe?

blocks.note: a cosmic trip is a journey through the universe
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A child left behind on a space voyage, snacking on peanuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peanuts' looks like snacks, but it is the Charles Schulz cartoon with Snoopy and Charlie Brown; the 'perhaps' shows it is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Peanuts is one instance of the newspaper cartoon form, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Burden we bear

definitions.note: read as ON US, a phrase, not a noun

blocks.note: a noun: a load or duty that someone has to carry
split the answer in two: a load we carry is placed upon ourselves

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as ON US: something that is on us is a weight we bear.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym for the first sense, a duty to be borne; the second sense is a split phrase, since a weight we bear is on us.

clue.text: American lawyer with bloody bad rash?

blocks.note: a DA is a district attorney, a US prosecutor
blood is red
evil means bad

explanation.surface: A US lawyer with a bad rash, and a swear word to go with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rash' looks like a skin complaint but is the adjective meaning reckless; the question mark hints at the Marvel hero Daredevil, a blind lawyer.
explanation.definitionFit: Daredevil, used as an adjective, means recklessly bold, rash.

clue.text: Curious stone inside mountain cut from behind

indicators.note: the stone sits inside the mountain

blocks.note: rum is an old British word for odd
a peak is a mountain
st is the abbreviation for stone, a British weight of 14 pounds

explanation.surface: An odd stone found inside a mountain, cut out from the back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut from behind' sounds like a quarrying method, but it is a cut of beef from the animal's hindquarters.
explanation.definitionFit: Rump steak is a cut of beef from the rump, the back end.

clue.text: Belligerent type, namely gangsta?

blocks.note: sc is short for scilicet, Latin for namely
a gangsta is a gangsta rapper

explanation.surface: A question: is the aggressive one just a gangster?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gangsta' looks like a street tough, which fits a belligerent type, but it stands for a performer of gangsta rap.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrapper is someone who likes a fight.

clue.text: Mice round when cooking is breach of standards

indicators.note: things being cooked are stirred and changed

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: Mice running round the kitchen during cooking break the hygiene rules.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a food-safety complaint, so 'standards' reads as hygiene rules, but the answer is a lapse in manners.
explanation.definitionFit: Indecorum is improper behaviour, a failure to keep to accepted standards.

clue.text: Reasons for writing less English

blocks.note: prose is ordinary writing
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: An argument for spending less time writing in English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reasons for' reads as the start of a sentence, but it is the definition: the pros are the points in favour.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: in 'pros and cons', the pros are the arguments in favour.

clue.text: Want expensive article reduced

indicators.note: the article is cut short by its last letter

blocks.note: dear means costly
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: Wanting a pricey item that has been marked down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Want' looks like a verb of desire, but it is a noun meaning lack.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, using the older noun sense of want: a lack or shortage, as in 'for want of'.

clue.text: President Bush battered dogfish to feed miserable lady at home

indicators.note: the dogfish is fed into the lady, going inside her

blocks.note: sad means miserable
a dame is a lady
huss is a British fishmonger's name for dogfish
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: A sorry scene at home: dogfish in batter served to a miserable lady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Battered' looks like the fish-and-chip shop sense, fish in batter, but it is the definition: the Iraqi president was attacked by President Bush.
explanation.definitionFit: Saddam Hussein was the Iraqi president whose country was attacked by US forces under both Presidents Bush.

clue.text: Animal that’s sometimes spotted chewing hay outside in Northamptonshire

indicators.note: something chewed is mashed up, so the letters are jumbled
only the outside letters of Northamptonshire are kept

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 3 letters
the first and last letters of Northamptonshire

explanation.surface: A farm animal, sometimes seen out in a field in Northamptonshire, chewing hay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside in' reads as a phrase about being out in the county, but 'outside' belongs to Northamptonshire and 'in' simply puts those letters in with HAY. Northamptonshire is an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: A description rather than a synonym: of the African scavengers, only one species has a spotted coat, the others being striped or brown.

clue.text: No more vessels capsized

indicators.note: a capsized vessel is upside down, and in a down answer that turns the word bottom to top

blocks.note: pots are vessels

explanation.surface: A report that no more ships remain afloat: they have all overturned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessels' suggests boats, which fits 'capsized', but here they are pots.
explanation.definitionFit: An interjection for interjection: shouted to end something, it means 'no more!'

clue.text: Line recess in church after concerning deterioration

blocks.note: re means concerning, as in a memo heading
L is the abbreviation for line
an apse is a rounded recess at the end of a church

explanation.surface: Lining a church recess after concerns about its crumbling state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line' looks like a verb, as in lining the recess, but it only gives L.
explanation.definitionFit: A relapse is a deterioration after an improvement, especially in health.

clue.text: Friend climbing pass when already ahead

indicators.note: in a down answer, climbing means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: A friend going up a mountain pass who is already in the lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass' looks like a mountain route to climb, but it is the verb in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To lap someone in a race is to pass them when you are already a full circuit ahead.

clue.text: Grave closest when moving north east

indicators.note: in an across answer, east is to the right

blocks.note: nearest means closest
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: A serious remark about which is closest when heading north-east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'North east' reads as a compass direction, but the north is the letter N and east says where it goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnest means serious, grave in manner.

clue.text: Book taxi on return, covered by yearly bonus

indicators.note: a taxi on its return trip goes back the other way
the taxi is covered by the bonus, so it sits inside it

blocks.note: pa is per annum, yearly
a cab is a taxi
a perk is a bonus on top of pay

explanation.surface: Booking a taxi for the return journey, paid for out of the annual bonus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' reads as the verb, booking a taxi, but it is the noun and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by genus: the answer is one kind of book, the soft-covered kind.

clue.text: Angry fellow returned plonk

blocks.note: a fellow is a he
to plonk something down is to put it

explanation.surface: A cross man sends back his cheap wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plonk' looks like the British word for cheap wine, which is why the fellow is angry, but it is the verb meaning to set down.
explanation.definitionFit: Het up is British informal for agitated or angry.
